source.title: HyperT5: Towards Compute-Efficient Korean Language Modeling
source.authors: Dongju Park; Soonwon Ka; Kang Min Yoo; Gichang Lee; Jaewoo Kang

record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation loss and fits a compute-optimal model-size trend in Korean seq2seq models, addressing scaling and compute-optimality claims with its own models and setup.
record.gate_note: Figure 3a reports validation-loss curves; Figure 3b and the text report the compute-optimal model-size fit. Table 3 reports downstream benchmark scores across HyperT5 sizes. Other reported results, including dialog adaptation and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, do not measure the scaling-law claims.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (Korean seq2seq T5.1.1 models, 97M–3B, 300B tokens), the authors run their own Hoffmann-style compute-optimality analysis. They fit a log-log line of optimal model size against compute (r2 = 0.988) and report downstream scores across the five sizes. Both bear on V3 (model-size part) and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that their largest model (3B) lies close to the predicted 5.6B optimum. They argue that decoder-only architectures scale better at larger budgets, while seq2seq is more cost-efficient below a compute threshold. They call the downstream advantage on NSMC preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: This is an industrial Korean seq2seq language-model study, not a reproduction of the original decoder-model scaling-law experiments. It performs a compute-optimality analysis similar to Hoffmann et al., using smoothed and interpolated loss curves and a small set of model sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: The optimality fit depends on smoothing and interpolation of loss curves and on choosing midpoint values for optimality segments; the authors state that the number of model-size samples is very small.

fits_no_version.finding: At the study's budget, the predicted compute-optimal size for seq2seq (5.6B) is far larger than a decoder-only reference line (448M). The authors infer that seq2seq is more efficient below a compute threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal model size and scaling efficiency depend on architecture (encoder-decoder vs decoder-only).

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Industry Track
record.problems: The compute-optimality analysis is based on a very small number of model-size samples, uses midpoint selection for optimality segments, and does not report uncertainty for its regression or prediction. Loss-curve values and exponents are not reported numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: None of the rows bearing on the listed versions were left out.

untested.parts: No loss power-law fit or exponents are reported. Tokens are fixed at 300B, with no data sweep.
The extrapolated optimal size (5.6B) and loss predictions for larger runs are never checked against actual larger runs.
The compute-optimal token-count trend and the parameter-vs-token growth rates are not reported. Kaplan vs Hoffmann is not compared.
Depth and width change together with size (Table 2). There is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
There is no scaling analysis for dialog adaptation or PEFT.
No alternative fitting choices or setups are compared for the study's own fit.

missing.what: mT5 (300M–3.7B) and KE-T5 (77M–783M) downstream scores across sizes, including non-monotone cases (mT5XL < mT5LARGE avg; KE-T5LARGE STS < BASE)

record.verdict_notes: The record called this T2; T3 is better because the method follows Hoffmann approach 1 in a new architecture and language setting. The reader's V3 limits_scope label (few samples, no token trend) mixes a method caveat with untested parts, so it is replaced by an untested entry. The decoder-only comparison line lacks a stated source. The PEFT (Table 4) and dialog (Tables 8–9) results across sizes are not scaling-law tests of pretraining loss.

versions.untested_parts: The study plots validation loss against FLOPs, but does not report explicit loss-law exponents or numerical curve values in the text. It holds pretraining tokens at 300B rather than testing a token-count sweep, and does not establish the stated several-orders-of-magnitude claim.
The extrapolation is of compute-optimal model size, not loss predictions from small runs to much larger runs.
The study fits optimal model size against compute for its seq2seq setup. It does not report a compute-optimal token-count trend or compare parameter and token growth rates.
No controlled comparison varies depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Dialog adaptation is reported, but no scaling-law analysis is conducted for it or another modality or training regime.
The study reports downstream benchmark scores by model size, but does not predict downstream performance from pretraining loss or fit a downstream scaling law.
The authors describe limited optimality data and their fitting procedure, but do not test whether alternative fitting choices or setups change the fitted laws.

relationships.condition: HyperT5 Korean seq2seq, 97M–3B, optimal model size vs compute
relationships.reason: Optimal model size follows a log-log linear trend in compute (r2 = 0.988), with a predicted 5.6B optimum (R6). This is based on few points with midpoint normalisation.
relationships.display_finding: A log-log linear fit achieved R²=0.988 and predicted a 5.6B optimum, using few points and midpoint normalization.

source_check.reason: R6: the log-log optimal-model-size regression has r2 = 0.988 and extrapolates a 5.6B optimum. This supports the parameter-count component; optimal token allocation is untested.

relationships.condition: HyperT5 family, all Table 3 tasks, fine-tuned
relationships.reason: Every task score and the average rise monotonically from 97M to 3B (avg 87.96→93.11). Gains shrink above 822M, and no predictive fit is given (R8–R42).
relationships.display_finding: Every task score increased with size and the average rose from 87.96 to 93.11, with diminishing gains above 822M and no predictive fit.
